pricing.freeTierCaps: $0; up to 1,000 subscribers and 4,000 sends/month; all features included with powered-by footer.
pricing.billingTerms: monthly only; no annual plan verified
pricing.hiddenCosts: Hard subscriber step-ups; Free includes powered-by footer.

verdictSummary: The visible SaaS email platform loop is buildable, but a credible replacement needs more than the first screen. Loops earns its keep through deliverability, reputation, network, so expect a weekend or multi-day build and a narrower personal scope.
coreLoopDIY: Build a small SaaS email platform editor and subscriber database that exports clean HTML and sends only through a reputable user-supplied email provider.
replacementScope: narrow personal or very small-team substitute
requirements: transactional or bulk email provider key in .env
whatYouLose: sender reputation, deliverability, and suppression handling
whyPeopleStillPay: Loops: The editor is trivial compared with inbox placement, compliance, reputation, unsubscribe handling, analytics, and audience growth infrastructure.
ongoingBurden: Own consent records, suppression lists, bounces, complaints, DNS, templates, accessibility, segmentation, and privacy requests.

priorArt.name: listmonk
priorArt.desc: High-performance self-hosted newsletter and mailing-list manager.

alternatives.name: Brevo Free
alternatives.desc: Hosted marketing and transactional email with automation; the 300-message daily cap is less startup-shaped.

facts.dataFormat: Contacts, campaigns, consent records, and message events live in Brevo's cloud; contacts can be exported as CSV.
facts.gapVsPaid: Brevo Free sends campaigns and transactional messages, but its 300-per-day throttle and less product-event-native workflow make it a poorer fit for SaaS lifecycle messaging than Loops.
facts.setupBlocker: Authenticating a custom sending domain requires adding DNS records.

alternatives.name: Dittofeed
alternatives.desc: Lifecycle journeys driven by product events, with richer branching and much heavier operations.

facts.install: Dittofeed Cloud or Docker Compose/Kubernetes self-host
facts.dataFormat: Self-hosted identity and configuration data lives in PostgreSQL and event/segment data in ClickHouse; optional blob data can use object storage.
facts.gapVsPaid: Dittofeed offers richer event-driven journeys, but PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, event instrumentation, and delivery-provider setup make it vastly heavier to operate than Loops.
facts.setupBlocker: Docker Compose brings Postgres and ClickHouse, but the harder first step is instrumenting product events and connecting an email provider.

alternatives.name: Loops Free
alternatives.desc: The vendor's own free tier includes every lifecycle and transactional feature for 1,000 contacts.

facts.dataFormat: Contacts, custom properties, events, workflows, and message history live in Loops' cloud; contacts can be imported/exported as CSV.
facts.gapVsPaid: Loops Free is the same product, but it stops being a full replacement once you exceed 1,000 contacts or 4,000 emails in a rolling 30-day period.
facts.setupBlocker: You must authenticate a sending domain and instrument your app or API before lifecycle emails become useful.

alternatives.name: Mautic
alternatives.desc: A complete lifecycle automation engine with no contact ceiling; simplicity left the building.

alternatives.name: Notifuse
alternatives.desc: Modern campaigns, transactional mail and visual automations in one compose stack; event collection remains your job.

facts.install: Notifuse Cloud signup or self-host with Docker
facts.dataFormat: Self-hosted contact, campaign, event, and analytics data lives in PostgreSQL; uploaded assets use S3-compatible storage.
facts.gapVsPaid: Notifuse provides campaigns, transactional mail, and visual automations, but product-event collection, infrastructure, and delivery configuration remain your responsibility.
facts.setupBlocker: Self-hosting needs Docker, PostgreSQL, object storage, a public domain, and a separately configured SMTP or email API provider.

alternatives.name: Plunk
alternatives.desc: Marketing, transactional email and workflows from one self-hosted app; SaaS-specific templates are fewer.

facts.dataFormat: Self-hosted data lives in PostgreSQL, queues in Redis, and uploads in bundled MinIO or another S3-compatible store.
facts.gapVsPaid: Plunk covers the same broad messaging modes, but it has fewer SaaS-specific templates and integrations and asks you to own the sending and operational stack.
facts.setupBlocker: The self-host path needs Docker, several subdomains, DNS/TLS, and an AWS SES account with credentials and domain verification.

notes: Useful boundary case: the first 60 percent of Loops is approachable, but operating the last 40 percent is the real subscription.
prompt:
Build a deliberately narrow personal substitute for Loops, not a full clone.
Use exactly this stack: Next.js 15 + TypeScript + PostgreSQL.
Primary job: Build a small SaaS email platform editor and subscriber database that exports clean HTML and sends only through a reputable user-supplied email provider.
Start from an empty folder and create the complete working project.
Make the default mode single-user and private.
Store user data locally unless the core job requires the declared self-hosted database.
Do not add analytics, telemetry, ads, or third-party accounts.
Put every secret and external credential in .env and provide .env.example.
Use realistic sample data that is clearly labelled and easy to delete.
Implement the smallest polished interface that completes the core loop end to end.
Include clear empty, loading, validation, success, and failure states.
Add import and export so the user is not trapped in the app.
Use accessible keyboard navigation, labels, focus states, and sensible contrast.
Validate untrusted input and never log secrets or private file contents.
Deliberately exclude these paid-product advantages: bounce, complaint, and suppression handling; large-scale segmentation and automation; payments, recommendations, and audience network.
Do not fake integrations, network effects, proprietary data, model quality, compliance, or security claims.
Where an external API is optional, keep the app useful without it and explain the degraded mode.
Write focused unit tests for the data model and the most important workflow.
Add one end-to-end smoke test that proves the core loop works.
Create a README with setup, permissions, architecture, data location, backup, and limitations.
Add scripts for install, development, test, build, and a production-style local run.
Run the tests and build before finishing, then fix errors rather than merely describing them.
